part.title: Nouns & cases
part.description: How nouns change: stems, the genitive, 'I have', the partitive, plurals, adjectives and consonant gradation.

topics.title: Noun stems: what happens before an ending
topics.summary: Before you add a case ending, many words change shape. A handful of patterns covers almost every word you'll meet.

sections.heading: Why stems matter
sections.body: Finnish has about 15 cases, but they all attach to the same **stem**. If you know the genitive (-n form) of a word, you know its stem: just remove the -n. *talon → talo-*, *huoneen → huonee-*, *naisen → naise-*.
sections.tip: When you learn a new noun, learn it as a pair: **basic form + genitive** (talo, talon · kieli, kielen · huone, huoneen).

sections.heading: The main patterns

rows: a, o, u, y, ä, ö

sections.note: Old -i words (kieli, ovi, järvi, lumi, nimi, uni, tuli, meri, pilvi, lehti…) must simply be learnt. New words and loans (kahvi, banaani, pankki, bussi, hotelli) keep the i.

sections.heading: Plus consonant gradation
sections.body: On top of the stem change, many words switch between a strong and weak consonant (kauppa → kaupassa, katu → kadulla). See [[kpt-nouns|Consonant gradation in nouns]].

topics.title: Genitive -n (of, 's)
topics.summary: The genitive ends in -n and means 'of' or 's: Pekan auto (Pekka's car), Suomen pääkaupunki (the capital of Finland).

sections.heading: Formation
sections.body: Stem + **-n**. Watch the stem (see [[word-stems|Noun stems]]) and K-P-T gradation (the -n closes the syllable, so the weak grade appears).

sections.heading: Uses
bullets: **Possession**: *Liisan koira* — Liisa's dog; *minun äitini* — my mother.
**'of'**: *Suomen pääkaupunki* — the capital of Finland; *talon katto* — the roof of the house.
**Before postpositions**: *talon edessä* — in front of the house; *pöydän alla* — under the table (see [[postpositions|Postpositions]]).
**'Whose?'** = *Kenen?*: *Kenen kirja tämä on? — Se on Annan kirja.*
**Total object** (a whole, finished thing): *Ostan auton.* — I (will) buy a/the car (see [[object-case|Object]]).

examples.fi: Minun isäni nimi on Juhani.
examples.en: My father's name is Juhani.

examples.fi: Pekan sisko asuu Turussa.
examples.en: Pekka's sister lives in Turku.

examples.fi: Kenen laukku tämä on? — Se on opettajan laukku.
examples.en: Whose bag is this? — It's the teacher's bag.

examples.fi: Suomen lippu on sininen ja valkoinen.
examples.en: Finland's flag is blue and white.

sections.heading: Plural genitive (for recognition)
sections.body: The plural genitive usually ends in **-den/-tten** or **-jen/-ien**: *talojen* (of the houses), *naisten* (of the women), *lasten* (of the children). You'll meet it in set phrases: *lasten huone* (children's room).

topics.title: My, your, his — possessives
topics.summary: minun kirja(ni), sinun kirja(si)… Possession is shown with a genitive pronoun and (in written Finnish) a possessive suffix.

sections.heading: The full pattern
bullets: The suffixes are **-ni, -si, -nsa/-nsä, -mme, -nne, -nsa/-nsä**.
With *minä, sinä, me, te* the pronoun can be dropped: *Kirjani on tässä.* (My book is here.)
Before a suffix the word takes its stem + weak/strong grade as in the genitive: *äiti → äitini*, *nimi → nimeni*, *huone → huoneeni*.
In everyday speech and in this course you can safely say **minun kirja** / **mun kirja**; recognise the suffixes when you read.

examples.fi: Mikä sinun nimesi on? — Minun nimeni on Gavin.
examples.en: What's your name? — My name is Gavin.

examples.fi: Tämä on minun perheeni.
examples.en: This is my family.

examples.fi: Hänen poikansa on opettaja.
examples.en: His/her son is a teacher.

examples.fi: Meidän talomme on vanha.
examples.en: Our house is old.

examples.fi: Kenen tämä puhelin on? — Se on minun.
examples.en: Whose phone is this? — It's mine.

examples.fi: Onko tämä sinun? — Ei, se on Pekan.
examples.en: Is this yours? — No, it's Pekka's.

topics.title: To have: minulla on
topics.summary: Finnish has no verb 'to have'. Instead: 'at me is' — Minulla on koira (I have a dog).

sections.heading: The structure: owner in -lla/-llä + on + thing
bullets: The verb is **always on** (3rd person singular) — even with *meillä* or *heillä*, even with plural things.
The owner goes into the **adessive** (-lla/-llä): *äiti → äidillä*, *Anna → Annalla*, *opettaja → opettajalla*.
Negative: **ei ole** + thing in the **partitive**: *Minulla ei ole autoa.*

examples.fi: Minulla on kaksi lasta.
examples.en: I have two children.

examples.fi: Onko sinulla sisaruksia? — On, minulla on yksi veli.
examples.en: Do you have siblings? — Yes, I have one brother.

examples.fi: Meillä ei ole koiraa, mutta meillä on kissa.
examples.en: We don't have a dog, but we have a cat.

examples.fi: Hänellä on siniset silmät ja pitkä tukka.
examples.en: He/she has blue eyes and long hair.

examples.fi: Minulla on nälkä / jano / kylmä / kuuma.
examples.en: I'm hungry / thirsty / cold / hot.

examples.fi: Minulla on flunssa. Minulla on päänsärky.
examples.en: I have the flu. I have a headache.

examples.fi: Minulla on kiire.
examples.en: I'm in a hurry.

sections.heading: Answering

examples.fi: Onko sinulla lemmikkiä? — On. / Ei ole.
examples.en: Do you have a pet? — Yes. / No.

sections.tip: Questions with 'onko … ?' often use the partitive for things you'd count: *Onko sinulla lapsia?* (any children?).

topics.title: Partitive singular
topics.summary: The partitive (-a/-ä, -ta/-tä, -tta/-ttä) is the 'some / part of / not whole' case — used after numbers, in negative sentences, for uncountables and with many verbs.

sections.heading: Endings — the rules from the course

rows: one short vowel (talo, kissa, kahvi, omena, leipä)
long vowel or diphthong (maa, tee, puu, tie)
-ta/-tä after l, n, r, s; otherwise -ea/-eä
kieltä, lunta, vettä · järveä, nimeä, ovea

sections.note: Partitive never takes the weak grade: *kauppa → kauppaa*, *äiti → äitiä* (strong grade, open syllable).

sections.heading: When to use it
bullets: **After numbers (2+)** and quantity words: *kaksi kahvia*, *paljon lunta*, *vähän rahaa*, *kilo omenoita*.
**Negative sentences**: *Minulla ei ole autoa.* *En juo kahvia.*
**Uncountable things** (mass nouns) — some, an amount: *Juon vettä.* *Ostan maitoa ja leipää.*
**Ongoing / unfinished action** and verbs that always take it: *rakastaa, odottaa, auttaa, ajatella, katsoa (TV), kuunnella, opiskella, harrastaa*: *Rakastan sinua. Odotan bussia. Opiskelen suomea.*
**Languages you speak**: *Puhun suomea.*
**Questions about having**: *Onko sinulla lapsia?*
**Describing uncountable subjects**: *Kahvi on kuumaa.* (the coffee is hot — material/mass)
**Greetings and wishes**: *Hyvää huomenta! Hyvää joulua!*

examples.fi: Saanko kupin kahvia ja palan kakkua?
examples.en: Can I have a cup of coffee and a piece of cake?

examples.fi: Haluaisin teetä ja kaksi pullaa.
examples.en: I'd like (some) tea and two buns.

examples.fi: Onko teillä gluteenitonta leipää?
examples.en: Do you have gluten-free bread?

examples.fi: Ei kiitos, en juo maitoa.
examples.en: No thanks, I don't drink milk.

topics.title: Plural: -t
topics.summary: The basic plural is stem + -t: talo → talot, kauppa → kaupat, huone → huoneet.

sections.heading: Nominative plural
sections.body: Take the genitive singular and replace **-n with -t**. So the stem and weak grade are the same as in the genitive.

sections.heading: When to use the -t plural
bullets: Specific, whole groups as subject: *Lapset leikkivät pihalla.* — The children are playing in the yard.

Things that come in pairs or sets are often plural in Finnish: *housut* (trousers), *farkut* (jeans), *sakset* (scissors), *silmälasit* (glasses), *häät* (wedding), *juhlat* (party), *synttärit* (birthday party).
Adjectives agree: *siniset silmät* (blue eyes), *mustat kengät* (black shoes).
After numbers you still use the **singular partitive**: *kaksi taloa* (not ✗taloja).

sections.heading: Plural in other cases (for recognition)
sections.body: Inside the plural, the marker is **-i-** (or -j- between vowels): *taloissa* (in the houses), *kaupoissa*, *kaduilla*, *huoneissa*. A short vowel before -i- often changes: a → o/–, ä → –, e → –: *kauppa → kaupoissa*, *kissa → kissoilla*, *päivä → päivinä*.

topics.title: Partitive plural
topics.summary: Some / many of a countable thing: omenoita (apples), kirjoja (books), lapsia (children).

sections.heading: Endings
sections.note: *kukka → kukkia is an exception to the o-rule. The partitive plural is one of the trickiest forms — learn the common ones as vocabulary: lapsia, omenoita, perunoita, mansikoita, kirjoja, kukkia, ystäviä, kenkiä, vaatteita, huoneita, naisia.

sections.heading: When
bullets: Indefinite amount of countable things: *Ostan omenoita.* — I'm buying (some) apples.
Negative and questions with plural meaning: *Onko sinulla lapsia? — Ei, minulla ei ole lapsia.*
After *paljon* (a lot) and *vähän* (a little): *Kaupassa on paljon ihmisiä.* (But *monta* + singular partitive: *monta ihmistä*.)
Plural 'are': *He ovat suomalaisia. Kengät ovat kalliita.*

topics.title: Adjectives, colours & describing people
topics.summary: Adjectives come before the noun and take the same case ending: iso talo → isossa talossa. Millainen hän on? describes people.

sections.heading: Agreement
sections.body: An adjective in front of a noun takes **the same case and number** as the noun.

rows: in front of the big house
The house is big. (no agreement needed after 'on')

sections.heading: Describing people — Millainen hän on?

rows: Hän on pitkä ja hoikka. Hän on iloinen ja ystävällinen.
Hänellä on lyhyt, vaalea tukka ja siniset silmät.
Hän on noin neljäkymmentä vuotta vanha.
Hänellä on päällä punainen takki ja mustat housut.

sections.tip: Appearance with 'have': *hänellä on* + plural nominative: *siniset silmät*, *pitkät hiukset*. Height and build with 'is': *hän on pitkä / lyhyt / hoikka / tukeva*.

sections.heading: Colours — Minkä värinen?

examples.fi: Minkä värinen sinun autosi on? — Se on punainen.
examples.en: What colour is your car? — It's red.

examples.fi: vaaleansininen / tummansininen
examples.en: light blue / dark blue (vaalea- light, tumma- dark)

sections.note: Colours ending in -nen inflect like *nainen*: *punaisessa talossa*, *punaista*, *punaiset*.

topics.title: Consonant gradation in nouns (K-P-T)
topics.summary: k, p and t change when a syllable closes: kauppa → kaupassa, katu → kadulla, Helsinki → Helsingissä.

sections.heading: Strong and weak grade
sections.body: The consonants **k, p, t** in the last syllable of a word have a *strong* and a *weak* form. Which one you use depends on whether the **syllable is open or closed** after the ending is added.
bullets: Open syllable (ends in a vowel) → **strong**: *kaup-pa*, *ka-tu*.
Closed syllable (ends in a consonant, e.g. -n, -t, -ssa, -lla) → **weak**: *kau-pan*, *ka-dun*, *kau-pas-sa*, *ka-dul-la*.
For basic-form words that end in a vowel, the basic form is strong and most endings make it weak.

rows: katu → kadulla, äiti → äidin, pöytä → pöydällä

sections.heading: Which endings make it weak?
sections.tip: Memory hook: the **partitive, illative and essive** keep the strong grade (their ending starts a new open syllable or lengthens the vowel); almost everything else is weak.

sections.heading: Reverse gradation: -e words
sections.body: Words ending in **-e** (and many in -as, -is, -in) work the other way round: the basic form is **weak** and the inflected forms are **strong**: **sade → sateen** (rain), **koe → kokeen** (test), **opas → oppaan** (guide), **rikas → rikkaan** (rich), **hammas → hampaan** (tooth), **lammas → lampaan** (sheep), **soitin → soittimen** (instrument), **keitin → keittimen** (kettle).
sections.note: The same reverse pattern happens in verb types 3 and 4: see [[kpt-verbs-3-4|K-P-T in verb types 3 & 4]].

examples.en: cow → cows · sheep → sheep (reverse: mm → mp) · goat → goats

topics.title: The object: genitive-n, partitive or nominative
topics.summary: A whole, finished object takes -n (Ostan auton); a partial, ongoing or negative one takes the partitive (Ostan maitoa, En osta autoa).

rows: En syö lihaa. — I don't eat meat.
Luen kirjaa. — I'm reading a book (not finished).
Luen kirjan. — I'll read the (whole) book.
Osta leipä! — Buy a loaf! · Syö omena! — Eat an apple!
Ostan liput. — I'll buy the tickets.

sections.heading: Verbs that always take the partitive
sections.body: Some verbs express ongoing feelings or activities and always take a partitive object: **rakastaa** (love), **odottaa** (wait for), **auttaa** (help), **ajatella** (think of), **harrastaa** (have as a hobby), **opiskella** (study), **soittaa** (play an instrument), **kuunnella** (listen to), **katsoa** (watch).

examples.fi: Odotan bussia.
examples.en: I'm waiting for the bus.

examples.fi: Harrastan joogaa ja hiihtoa.
examples.en: My hobbies are yoga and skiing.

examples.fi: Soitan kitaraa.
examples.en: I play the guitar.
